summary: Brompton Cemetery is a garden cemetery in West Brompton, London. It lies in the Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea. Since 1852 it has been London's only Crown-owned cemetery. The Royal Parks manages it. It is one of London's "Magnificent Seven" cemeteries. Private companies founded these as inner-city churchyards overflowed. An 1837 Act of Parliament authorised it. It was laid out in 1839 and opened in 1840. Architect Benjamin Bauda designed it like an open-air cathedral. It has a domed chapel and long colonnades. Catacombs below the colonnades sold only about 500 places. Building costs overran, and early burials were few. An 1850 Act let the government buy such cemeteries. About 35,000 monuments mark over 205,000 graves. The site is listed Grade I. It was the London District's military cemetery from 1854 to 1939. It was closed to most burials from 1952 to 1996. It is a working cemetery again. It is known as an urban haven for nature. A National Lottery-funded restoration ran from 2014 to 2018.
